title: Chaukhamba (7,138 m): The Four Pillars of Garhwal
seo_title: Chaukhamba (7,138 m): Facts, Routes & Climbing History
seo_desc: Chaukhamba, Garhwal: all four summits with heights, the Gangotri glacier link, the 1952 first ascent, the route camp by camp and its 2026 permit status.
label: Chaukhamba
blurb: 7,138 m · the four pillars above the Gangotri glacier
tag: Four pillars of ice at the head of the Gangotri glacier.
sub: Chaukhamba is a wall of four summits west of Badrinath, and Chaukhamba I at 7,138 m is the highest peak of the Gangotri group. Here are all four with their heights, the glaciers it feeds, the route camp by camp, how dangerous the climb is, the 2026 permit status and the story from the 1952 first ascent to the 2024 helicopter rescue.

q: How high is Chaukhamba, and where is it?
answer: Chaukhamba is a massif of four summits in the Garhwal Himalaya of Uttarakhand, west of Badrinath. The highest, Chaukhamba I, is 7,138 m (23,419 ft), the top of the Gangotri group, and the Gangotri glacier rises on its north-western slopes. The name means "four pillars". It was first climbed on 13 June 1952. See all 7,000 m peaks in India.

intro: Status, checked 18 November 2026: open. The "Chaukhamba group" is named in the list of 83 peaks that Uttarakhand opened on 4 February 2026. Indian climbers apply on the state's UKMPS portal and pay no state fees in 2026; foreign teams pay only the IMF fees. We found no closure order since.

Four pillars on one ridge. Chaukhamba means "four pillars", for the four summits that stand in a line on a north-east to south-west ridge. The main summit, Chaukhamba I, is at the north-east end; the heights of all four are in the four pillars table below. The massif rises 1,594 m above its key col at Mana Pass, which makes it an ultra-prominent peak.

Where the Ganga's glacier begins. Chaukhamba stands above three glaciers: the Gangotri, the Bhagirathi Kharak and the Satopanth. The Gangotri glacier, the source of the Bhagirathi, rises on its north-western slopes, and the Satopanth glacier links it to Satopanth (7,075 m). For the wider picture, read our Indian Himalaya guide, the highest peaks in Uttarakhand and the full list of India's highest peaks.
route_h2: The route to Chaukhamba I, camp by camp
route_text: From Badrinath, up the Bhagirathi Kharak glacier. The first ascent in 1952 and the 2022 solo climb both came from the north-east side. The road ends at Badrinath, at about 3,300 m. Base camp sits at the fork of the Bhagirathi Kharak glacier at 4,627 m, about five days from the road. In 1952 the summit team climbed the north-east face from a high camp at about 5,950 m.

The 1952 line on the north face is described today as no longer practicable, and the north flank as very dangerous. In 2001 an Indian team climbing from Badrinath had its Camp 3 at 6,350 m; an avalanche hit that camp. Later climbers have used the north-east ridge.

The west side is reached from Gangotri and Gaumukh: a 2004 team put base camp at about 4,900 m where the Swachand glacier meets the Gangotri glacier. Camp heights change from year to year. No official itinerary exists; about four weeks from the road-head is a fair estimate.

About five days up the valley to base camp at the Bhagirathi Kharak glacier fork, 4,627 m.
Load carries and fixed rope towards a high camp near 6,000 m, sleeping high and coming back down.
From the high camp up the north-east side to the 7,138 m summit plateau, then down the fixed lines.
Weather days and the walk out
Spare days for snow and wind, then clearing the camps and the walk back to Badrinath.
difficulty_h2: How hard is it to climb Chaukhamba?
difficulty: Our dataset grades Chaukhamba I technical. It is a full expedition above 7,000 m, and the record shows real danger: avalanches and rockfall on the north side, an avalanche that killed two climbers at Camp 3 in 2001, and a three-day ordeal on Chaukhamba III in October 2024 that ended with an Indian Air Force rescue.

Arrive with at least one earlier summit above 6,000 m and solid fixed-rope and glacier skills. In Himachal, good steps towards a peak like this are Deo Tibba (6,001 m), Mulkila (6,517 m) and Reo Purgyil (6,816 m). Read our altitude sickness guide before you go high.
skills: At least one summit above 6,000 m and days on crevassed glaciers.
Crampons and ice axe on steep snow and ice, fixed ropes, jumaring, abseiling and crevasse rescue.
Repeated load carries between camps and a long summit day near 7,000 m.
Reading avalanche slopes and fresh snow, and the discipline to turn back.
A Basic and an Advanced Mountaineering Course; Indian teams also follow IMF rules on team qualifications.
season_text: May to June and September to October. The recorded climbs fit those windows: the first ascent on 13 June 1952 and the Korean ascent of Chaukhamba II on 14 May 1996. The October 2024 rescue shows that autumn weather can still turn fast at 6,000 m.
July and August are monsoon months in Garhwal. Our best time for mountaineering in India guide compares the seasons region by region.
permits: Indian climbers apply on Uttarakhand's UKMPS portal. The Chaukhamba group is on the state's February 2026 list of 83 open peaks, and all state fees are waived for Indian climbers in 2026. IMF rules for Indian teams still apply.

Foreign nationals need IMF permission, with a liaison officer and insurance. Chaukhamba I and II are above 7,000 m, where the IMF base fee is US$1,000 for a team of two, plus US$500 for liaison-officer equipment, and per-member charges apply; Chaukhamba III and IV fall in the 6,501–7,000 m band (US$700) (IMF peak-fee page, as of 1 Oct 2026). More in our IMF permit and peak fees guide and mountaineering in India for foreign climbers.
The west approach from Gaumukh lies inside Gangotri National Park; park entry is arranged with the expedition permit.
gear: Insulated mountaineering boots rated for 7,000 m and above, with crampons
A mountaineering ice axe, a jumar (ascender) and a descender
Climbing harness, helmet, carabiners and slings
Down suit or heavy down jacket, and a sleeping bag for −25 °C or colder
Windproof and waterproof shell jacket and trousers
Headlamp with spare batteries for the pre-dawn start
Trekking poles for the walk-in to base camp
Two insulated water bottles and a personal first-aid kit
history: 1938 and 1939: the first attempts on Chaukhamba failed.

13 June 1952: Lucien George and Victor Russenberger, Swiss members of a French expedition led by E. Frendo, made the first ascent of Chaukhamba I by the north-east face from the Bhagirathi Kharak glacier, starting from a high camp at about 5,950 m.

1995: a team of instructors from the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering, led by Col M.P. Yadav, climbed Chaukhamba I by the west face and made the first ascent of Chaukhamba II. 1996: the Garhwal Rifles climbed Chaukhamba I by the south-west face, and on 14 May a Korean team made the second ascent of Chaukhamba II by the north-west ridge.

2001: an Indian expedition from Badrinath lost two members when an avalanche hit Camp 3 at 6,350 m. 2004: a Nehru Institute team tried Chaukhamba III and IV from the Gangotri side and reached about 6,300 m.
2022: Boris Textor climbed Chaukhamba I solo by the north-east ridge, reaching it by the left side of the north face; his GPS read 7,136 m on top.

October 2024: two foreign women climbers, one American and one British, were stranded at about 6,015 m on Chaukhamba III after losing their food and gear. A French team found them on 5 October, and Indian Air Force helicopters lifted them to Joshimath on 6 October. February 2026: the Chaukhamba group was named in Uttarakhand's list of 83 opened peaks.

extra_sections.h2: The four Chaukhamba summits and their heights
extra_sections.html:
The four summits stand in a line from north-east to south-west, with the highest at the north-east end. Only Chaukhamba I is in our dataset of India's peaks; the other heights are the commonly published figures.

SummitHeightWhat we know
Chaukhamba I7,138 m / 23,419 ftFirst ascent 13 Jun 1952, north-east face; west face 1995; south-west face 1996
Chaukhamba II7,070 m / 23,196 ftFirst ascent 1995, Nehru Institute of Mountaineering team; second ascent 14 May 1996, Korean team, north-west ridge
Chaukhamba IIIabout 6,990 m / 22,930 ftPublished as 6,995 m; the Himalayan Journal gives 6,974 m. Site of the October 2024 rescue
Chaukhamba IV6,854 m / 22,487 ftA 2004 attempt on III and IV from the Gangotri side reached about 6,300 m

extra_sections.label: Gangotri glacier
extra_sections.html:
Chaukhamba is the highest point of the Gangotri group. The Gangotri glacier, the source of the Bhagirathi, rises on its north-western slopes. The Bhagirathi Kharak and Satopanth glaciers lie on its other flanks, and the Satopanth glacier links it to Satopanth peak.

That is why the peak has two ways in: from Gangotri and Gaumukh on the west, inside Gangotri National Park, and from Badrinath on the east. For other Garhwal giants, see Shivling (6,543 m) and Kamet (7,756 m).

faqs: What is the height of Chaukhamba?
Chaukhamba I, the highest of its four summits, is 7,138 m (23,419 ft). The other three are Chaukhamba II (7,070 m), III (about 6,990 m) and IV (6,854 m).
Chaukhamba means "four pillars", for the four summits that stand in a line on one ridge.
In the Garhwal Himalaya of Uttarakhand, west of Badrinath, at the head of the Gangotri glacier. It is the highest peak of the Gangotri group.
The Gangotri glacier, the source of the Bhagirathi, rises on Chaukhamba's north-western slopes.
Lucien George and Victor Russenberger, Swiss members of a French expedition, reached the summit of Chaukhamba I on 13 June 1952 by the north-east face.
Is Chaukhamba open for climbing in 2026?
Yes. The Chaukhamba group is on Uttarakhand's February 2026 list of 83 opened peaks. Indian climbers apply on the UKMPS portal with no state fees; foreign teams apply through the IMF.
It is a technical expedition above 7,000 m with avalanche and rockfall danger; the north flank is described as very dangerous. Climbers need an earlier 6,000 m summit and mountaineering training.
What happened on Chaukhamba III in 2024?
Two foreign women climbers were stranded at about 6,015 m for three days after losing their food and gear. Indian Air Force helicopters rescued them on 6 October 2024.
